9790:
Laudatory means expressing praise or strong admiration for someone or something.

When something is described as laudatory, it means it contains enthusiastic, positive, and complimentary words about a person, thing, or achievement. Think of it this way: if you walk away from reading or hearing something feeling like the person behind it was being celebrated or glorified, that thing was laudatory.

The simplest way to understand it: laudatory = full of praise.

Anything can be laudatory — a speech, a review, an article, a letter, a comment, or even a gesture — as long as its main purpose or tone is to praise someone or something.

This is important: laudatory is not weak or mild praise. It is not merely saying something is "okay" or "decent." Laudatory language is warm, enthusiastic, and clearly admiring. It goes beyond a polite compliment into genuine, often deliberate celebration of someone's qualities, work, or achievements.

Imagine the difference between a friend saying "Yeah, your cooking was pretty good" versus "That was the most incredible meal I've ever had — you have a real gift." The second one is laudatory.

Here are examples that show the word in action so you can feel exactly how it is used:

  • The professor gave a laudatory speech about the student who won the scholarship, praising her dedication and brilliance.
    → The speech was full of praise and admiration.
  • The film critic wrote a laudatory review of the director's latest work, calling it a masterpiece of modern cinema.
    → The review was overwhelmingly positive and celebratory.
  • His boss sent a laudatory email to the entire company, highlighting how his efforts had saved the project.
    → The email was meant to publicly praise and honor him.
  • The biography was so laudatory that it barely mentioned any of the leader's flaws.
    → The book was so full of praise that it felt one-sided.
  • She was embarrassed by the laudatory remarks made about her at the award ceremony.
    → The remarks were so glowing and complimentary that they made her uncomfortable.

Laudatory is most naturally used in formal or semi-formal contexts — think reviews, speeches, letters of recommendation, award ceremonies, public tributes, and official statements. You wouldn't typically use it to describe a friend casually saying something nice. It carries a slightly elevated, ceremonial flavor.

Also — and this is subtle — when someone calls something "laudatory," they are describing the tone or nature of the praise, not necessarily agreeing with it. For example:

  • The review was laudatory, but many readers felt the praise was exaggerated.

Here, the writer is telling you the review was full of praise without saying that praise was deserved. So "laudatory" is a neutral descriptor of tone. It simply tells you praise is happening — it doesn't tell you whether that praise is earned or fair.

• It is not neutral. A balanced or mixed review is not laudatory.
  • It is not subtle. Faint praise or a lukewarm compliment is not laudatory.
  • It is not critical. A laudatory piece does not focus on flaws, failures, or shortcomings. If it does, it's no longer laudatory.
Words That Are Similar (and How Laudatory Differs)

Understanding related words will sharpen your grasp of this one:

  • Complimentary — also means expressing praise, but it's softer, more everyday, and less formal. A complimentary comment is nice; a laudatory speech is an event.
  • Flattering — suggests praise that may make someone feel good, but often carries a hint that the praise might be excessive or not entirely sincere.
  • Glowing — a very close synonym. A "glowing review" and a "laudatory review" mean nearly the same thing. "Glowing" is more common in everyday speech; "laudatory" is more formal.
  • Eulogistic — means very highly praising, often specifically for the dead (like in a eulogy). Laudatory is broader and applies to the living too.
  • Adulatory — means extremely, sometimes excessively admiring — almost worshipful. It's a stronger and more intense version of laudatory, and often carries a sense of going overboard.
The opposite would be words like critical, disparaging, censorious, condemnatory, or derogatory — all of which involve negative judgment rather than praise.

Here's a simple memory anchor: think of the word "laud" sitting right inside laudatory. To laud someone means to praise them highly. So laudatory simply means of, relating to, or full of that kind of high praise. Whenever you see the word, picture someone standing at a podium delivering a glowing, celebratory tribute — that is the spirit of laudatory.

What it meansExpressing strong praise or admiration
Used to describeSpeeches, reviews, articles, letters, remarks, tributes
ToneWarm, enthusiastic, celebratory, formal
DegreeStrong praise — not mild or lukewarm
Key nuanceDescribes the nature of praise, not whether it's deserved
OppositeCritical, derogatory, disparaging
9791:
When someone or something is described as lauded, it means they have received a great deal of enthusiastic, public praise — often from many people, or from respected and influential voices.

Think of it this way: if being "praised" is a 6 out of 10, being "lauded" is a 9 or 10. The word carries a sense of remarkable, notable acclaim — not just polite appreciation, but genuine, widespread admiration.

When you call something lauded, you are communicating three things at once:

1. The praise is strong. It is not vague or half-hearted. People have spoken highly and admiringly.

2. The praise is wide. It usually comes from many people, or from people whose opinions carry weight — critics, experts, the public, respected institutions. One person's admiration does not make something "lauded."

3. The praise is known. The acclaim is visible and public enough that it has become a recognised fact about that person or thing. The word almost serves as a badge — it tells you that the praise has been noted and acknowledged.
What can be described as lauded?

Almost anything that can receive praise:

  • A person: a lauded scientist, a lauded chef, a lauded poet
  • A creative work: a lauded novel, a lauded film, a lauded album
  • A performance: a lauded stage debut, a lauded speech
  • An achievement or effort: a lauded conservation programme, a lauded policy

"The lauded author returned to her hometown to give a talk at the local school."

Here, the author has been extensively and publicly praised — likely by critics, readers, or literary institutions. Calling her "lauded" immediately signals her high reputation before you even learn her name.

"His lauded performance in the film earned him three major award nominations."

The performance has been widely admired and spoken of highly. The word tells you, in a single breath, that the praise is not just one person's view — it is broadly recognised.

"The company launched its lauded wellness programme across all its offices."

The programme has received notable praise, perhaps from employees, media, or industry observers. Using "lauded" here adds credibility and weight to the programme before you even describe it.
The tone and register of the word

"Lauded" is a formal, slightly literary word. You will encounter it most often in:

  • Newspaper and magazine writing
  • Book and film reviews
  • Biographies and profiles
  • Speeches and official writing
  • Academic or intellectual contexts

In everyday conversation, people rarely say "lauded." They would more likely say "well-known," "highly praised," or "amazing." So if you encounter "lauded" in speech, it usually signals that the speaker is being deliberate and careful with language, or speaking in a formal setting.

Most of the time, "lauded" is used straightforwardly and positively. But writers sometimes use it with a slight detachment — almost as if to say, "widely praised, though I am not personally endorsing that praise."

For example:

"The much-lauded economic reforms did little to help ordinary citizens."

Here, the writer acknowledges that the reforms were widely praised, but the sentence then pushes back against that praise. The word "lauded" signals: this is what others said — without the writer fully agreeing.

This ironic or distancing use is not the primary meaning, but it is a real possibility. When you see "lauded" followed by a critical or disappointing outcome, that is likely what is happening.
How lauded compares to similar words

Acclaimed is the closest synonym — nearly interchangeable with "lauded." Both suggest strong, public, recognised praise. If anything, "acclaimed" is slightly more common and neutral; "lauded" can feel a touch more emphatic.

Celebrated is similar, but it leans more toward fame and wide recognition rather than the specific act of being praised. A celebrated person is famous and admired; a lauded person has been actively and enthusiastically commended.

Renowned simply means widely known and respected — it does not specifically emphasise praise the way "lauded" does.

Esteemed means deeply respected, but more quietly and personally. Esteemed lacks the public, vocal dimension that "lauded" carries.

Praised is the plain, everyday version. "Lauded" is what "praised" becomes when the praise is exceptional in scale and enthusiasm.
The single clearest way to remember it

Lauded = the kind of praise that is strong enough, wide enough, and public enough to become a recognised fact about someone or something.

If you can replace "lauded" in a sentence with "widely and enthusiastically praised" and the meaning holds perfectly — you have understood the word completely.
9792: A laughingstock is a person (or sometimes a thing) that everyone laughs at, mocks, or ridicules — usually because they have done something embarrassing, foolish, or have some quality that others find deeply amusing or pathetic.

Imagine a person who does something so embarrassing — or fails at something so completely — that people don't just laugh once and move on. Instead, they keep talking about it. The person becomes famous for being laughed at. They become, in everyone's eyes, a symbol of foolishness or failure. That person is a laughingstock.

The word carries a strong sense of public humiliation. It's not about a quiet, private embarrassment. It's about being the subject of widespread mockery — the kind where people point, whisper, and shake their heads. Being called a laughingstock is deeply unflattering.

This is an important detail: a laughingstock is not someone who gets a light chuckle. The mockery is widespread and often sustained. People don't just snicker — they openly ridicule. And it's not just one or two people laughing; it's a group, a crowd, a community, or even an entire country.

Think of these scales:

  • A student who confidently gives a wildly wrong answer in front of the whole class might become the laughingstock of the class.
  • A company that launches a product with a terrible, embarrassing flaw might become the laughingstock of the industry.
  • A politician who makes a spectacularly foolish mistake might become the laughingstock of the country — or even the world.

Usually, it's one of these:

  • A public failure — especially one that was avoidable or self-caused (e.g., a team that was expected to win and loses catastrophically).
  • Hypocrisy exposed — someone who preached one thing and was caught doing the opposite.
  • Arrogance meeting reality — someone who boasted too loudly and then failed spectacularly.
  • Genuinely absurd behaviour — actions so foolish or ridiculous that they invite ridicule.

The common thread is that the ridicule feels deserved to those doing the laughing — even if it isn't always fair.
Tone and weight of the word

"Laughingstock" is a strong word. It signals more than just embarrassment — it signals a loss of dignity and respect in the eyes of others. When you call someone a laughingstock, you're saying: people don't take them seriously anymore; they've become a joke.

It can be used:

  • Critically, to describe someone who has genuinely humiliated themselves.
  • Sympathetically, to warn someone or describe their unfortunate situation.
  • As a threat or warning — "If you do that, you'll make us the laughingstock of the city."

• "After the disastrous press conference, the CEO became the laughingstock of the business world."
  • "Don't wear that to school — you'll be the laughingstock of the whole grade."
  • "The team's 10–0 loss made them the laughingstock of the league."
  • "He used to be respected, but after that scandal, he's now just a laughingstock."

Notice the common pattern: "the laughingstock of [some group]." This is the most natural and frequent way the word appears. You almost always attach it to a group of people who are doing the laughing.

A laughingstock isn't always someone who intended to be funny. In fact, it's usually the opposite — the person was being serious, but others found them ridiculous. There's a painful irony in it: the person is laughed at, not laughed with. This is what makes the word carry such a sting.

A laughingstock is someone who has become an object of widespread, open mockery — usually because of a public failure, foolishness, or embarrassment so notable that people remember it and keep talking about it. The word is always negative, always implies lost respect, and almost always refers to ridicule that happens in front of, or within, a recognizable group.
9793: The verb to launder means to clean something — but not just physically. It carries a deeper sense: making something look acceptable, respectable, or legitimate when it originally wasn't. This idea runs through both its literal and figurative uses.
1. The Literal Meaning — Washing Clothes or Linens

In its most basic sense, to launder means to wash fabrics — clothes, bed sheets, towels, tablecloths, and similar items.

"Please launder these shirts before the event."
"The hotel launders its bedsheets daily."

This is slightly more formal than just saying "wash." When someone says launder, it often implies a complete cleaning process — washing, drying, and possibly pressing or ironing — rather than a quick rinse. You'll see this word on clothing care labels, in hotel contexts, and in formal or professional settings.

In everyday speech, most people just say "wash my clothes" — but launder is the precise, complete term for the full process.

This is the meaning you'll encounter far more often in news, books, films, and conversation. To launder money means to take money that was obtained illegally and pass it through a process that makes it appear to have come from a legitimate, legal source.

Think of it this way:

Imagine a criminal earns millions of rupees through illegal activity — say, drug trafficking. They can't simply walk into a bank and deposit this cash. The bank and the government would ask: where did this money come from? They have no honest answer. So the money is "dirty" — it carries the stain of its illegal origin.

To solve this problem, the criminal launders the money. They run it through a legitimate-looking business — a restaurant, a construction company, a car wash — and mix the illegal cash in with real business income. Now, when they deposit the money, it appears to be regular earnings from a legal business. The illegal origin has been hidden. The money is now "clean."

The metaphor is direct and deliberate: just as laundering removes dirt from clothes, money laundering removes the criminal "stain" from money.

"The gang laundered millions through a chain of restaurants."
"He was arrested for laundering drug money through offshore accounts."

The noun form of this process is money laundering.

How it typically works (simplified):

There are usually three stages, though you don't need to memorize the technical terms — just the idea:

  1. Placement — The illegal cash is introduced into the financial system somehow (deposited in small amounts, used to buy assets, etc.)
  2. Layering — The money is moved around in complex ways — transferred between accounts, converted into different currencies, sent through multiple countries — to make it difficult to trace back to its origin.
  3. Integration — The money re-enters the economy looking completely clean and legitimate, often as business income, investments, or property purchases.

The entire goal is to break the traceable link between the money and the crime that produced it.

Because "launder" carries the idea of disguising or cleaning up something tainted, it gets used metaphorically in other contexts too:

Reputation laundering — When a disgraced person, company, or country tries to restore its public image by associating with respected institutions, causes, or figures, often without genuinely changing their behavior.

"Critics accused the billionaire of using charity donations to launder his reputation."

Information or narrative laundering — When false, misleading, or propaganda content is passed through seemingly credible sources to make it appear trustworthy.

"The disinformation was laundered through fake academic websites before spreading to mainstream media."

In all these cases, the underlying meaning is the same: something tainted or problematic is run through a process designed to make it appear clean, legitimate, or credible.

• Laundering always implies concealment. There is always something being hidden — the origin, the true nature, the problem. It is never a neutral act.
  • In the financial sense, laundering is always illegal. You cannot launder legitimately earned money — that would just be depositing it normally.
  • The word carries moral weight. Calling something "laundered" is a serious accusation. It implies deception, criminal intent, or at minimum unethical behavior.
  • The literal use (clothes) is formal and complete. When you say a garment has been laundered, you mean it has been thoroughly cleaned and is presentable — it's a higher-care word than simply "washed."

UseWhat's being "cleaned"Why
LiteralClothes, linensTo make them physically clean and presentable
FinancialIllegal moneyTo hide its criminal origin and make it look legitimate
MetaphoricalReputation, informationTo disguise something tainted as respectable or credible

To launder is to clean — but cleaning here is always about appearances, concealment, and making something unacceptable look acceptable. Whether it's a dirty shirt or dirty money, the goal is the same: present it to the world as something respectable.
9794: A laundromat is a business — open to any member of the public — that contains rows of washing machines and dryers that customers pay to use themselves. You walk in with dirty clothes, operate the machines on your own, pay a fee, and walk out with clean, dry laundry. Nobody does the laundry for you; that is the defining feature of a laundromat: it is entirely self-service.

Step into a laundromat and you'll typically see:

  • Rows of front-loading or top-loading washing machines in various sizes — standard, large, and extra-large
  • Dryers lined up nearby
  • Folding tables in the middle or along one side, for sorting and folding clothes once they're done
  • A change machine that converts paper bills into coins
  • Vending machines selling laundry detergent, fabric softener, dryer sheets, and sometimes snacks or drinks
  • Seating (benches or chairs) for customers who wait while their clothes run

Some modern laundromats are clean and updated, with Wi-Fi and TV screens. Others are more basic. Size can vary from a small room with 8–10 machines to a large hall with 50 or more.

Traditionally, machines in a laundromat are coin-operated — you insert coins (typically quarters in the United States) to start and run them. This is why laundromats are also commonly called coin laundries or coin-op laundromats. In more modern facilities, payment is made by swiping a debit/credit card, using a mobile app, or loading money onto a reusable card issued by the laundromat.

Pricing is per machine per load, and it varies based on machine size. Larger machines (useful for bulky items) cost more. Washing and drying are typically paid for separately.
How the process works, step by step

1. You arrive with your dirty laundry in a bag or basket.
  2. You find an available washing machine and check its size (match it to how much laundry you have — overfilling a machine cleans poorly).
  3. You load your clothes in, add detergent (bring your own or buy it from the vending machine there), select your wash settings, and pay.
  4. The machine runs automatically — typically 25 to 45 minutes — while you wait.
  5. Once washing is done, you move the wet clothes to a dryer, pay again, and set the drying time.
  6. After the dryer finishes, you take your clothes to a folding table, fold or roll them, pack up, and leave.

The entire visit usually takes between 1 and 2 hours, depending on how many loads you have.
Why it is NOT the same as a dry cleaner

This distinction confuses some learners. A dry cleaner is a business where you drop off your clothes, and trained staff clean them for you using special chemical processes — you pick them up later, cleaned and pressed. You don't touch the machines at all.

A laundromat is the opposite: you do all the work yourself. There are no staff cleaning your clothes. You are essentially renting access to the machines.

Some laundromats do offer an optional "wash-and-fold" service — you drop off a bag of laundry, and staff wash, dry, and fold it for you for an extra fee. But this is an add-on service, not the main model. The default nature of a laundromat is always self-service.
Who uses a laundromat, and why

• People who live in apartments or rented homes that don't have their own washer and dryer
  • People who are traveling (backpackers, road-trippers, long-stay tourists) who need to freshen up their clothes
  • People who need to wash large or bulky items — thick comforters, sleeping bags, heavy blankets, or rugs — that won't fit in a standard home machine. Laundromats usually have industrial-sized machines built for exactly this
  • People whose home machine is broken and need a temporary solution
  • People who simply find it more economical not to own a washer and dryer

Some laundromats have a staff member called an attendant who is present during operating hours. Their job is to help customers use the machines, collect payment, keep the place clean, and address any problems (like a machine eating your money). Other laundromats are entirely unattended — there is no staff at all, and the place may be open 24 hours. You are on your own, operating the machines by reading the posted instructions.
Other names for the same thing

• Launderette (also spelled laundrette) — the standard British English term for exactly the same place. If you're reading a British novel and see "launderette," it means a laundromat.
  • Coin laundry — used in some parts of Asia and informally in the US
  • Coin-op laundry — short for coin-operated laundry
  • Public laundry — a more general, less common term

In American English, "laundromat" is by far the most common and recognized word.

• "My building doesn't have laundry facilities, so I go to the laundromat around the corner every Sunday."
  • "She spent the afternoon at the laundromat, reading a novel while her clothes tumbled in the dryer."
  • "All the large machines at the laundromat were taken, so he had to split his comforter load into two."
  • "On his cross-country road trip, he stopped at a laundromat in Kansas to wash a week's worth of clothes."
  • "The laundromat charges $3.50 for a standard wash cycle and $0.25 for every 8 minutes of drying time."
The one-sentence definition to remember forever
A laundromat is a self-service, pay-per-use public facility with washing machines and dryers where anyone can come in off the street, do their own laundry for a fee, and leave.
9795:
A laureate is a person who has been officially and formally honored for outstanding achievement — usually by a prestigious institution, government, or organization. The honor recognizes that this person has reached the highest level of excellence in their particular field.

Think of it this way: millions of people might be good at science, literature, or poetry. But a laureate is someone who has been looked at by the most respected authorities and officially declared: "This person's work is so exceptional, it deserves our highest recognition."

Two things must be true for someone to be called a laureate:

1. The recognition must be official. A laureate isn't just someone who is famous or popular. They've received a formal honor — awarded by an institution that has the authority and reputation to give it. Public admiration alone doesn't make you a laureate.

2. The honor must be prestigious. Not every award makes someone a laureate. The word is reserved for the highest tier of recognition — the kind of award that defines a person's life and legacy.

If someone wins a local writing contest, they are a winner. If someone is awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature, they are a laureate. The difference is the weight and stature of the recognition.

1. Nobel Laureate

This is the most widely used form of the word today. A Nobel Laureate is someone who has won a Nobel Prize — arguably the most respected award in the world — in fields like Physics, Chemistry, Medicine, Literature, Economics, or Peace.

Marie Curie is a Nobel Laureate in Physics and also in Chemistry — she won the prize twice.

When a new Nobel Laureate is announced each year, the world pays attention.

The title "Nobel Laureate" stays with the person for life. Even decades after winning, they are still referred to by that title.

2. Poet Laureate

A Poet Laureate is an officially appointed poet — chosen by a government (national or regional) to represent that country's or region's poetic tradition. It's an official position, not just an award. The Poet Laureate may be asked to write poems for national occasions, ceremonies, or significant events.

The United States has a Poet Laureate, appointed by the Library of Congress.

The United Kingdom also has a Poet Laureate, a tradition that goes back centuries.

Being named Poet Laureate means your peers and your country's highest institutions have declared you the finest or most distinguished poet among them.

The word isn't limited to Nobel Prizes and poets. It can appear anywhere a formal, high-level honor is given:

  • A country may give its top artists or scientists a laureate title.
  • Some universities grant the title of laureate to exceptional honorary graduates.
  • International competitions in music, science, and the arts sometimes call their top winners laureates.

The word travels with prestige. Wherever you see it, it signals: this person has been recognized at the very top.
How It Feels in a Sentence

The word most naturally appears as part of a compound title or phrase:

  • "As a Nobel Laureate, she was invited to address the United Nations."
  • "The Poet Laureate recited an original poem at the inauguration."
  • "He is one of the youngest laureates in the history of the prize."

Notice that "laureates" (plural) is simply used when referring to multiple such honored people.

This is important, because the word has a very specific weight:

  • A laureate is not simply a famous person. Fame can exist without formal recognition.
  • A laureate is not just someone who won any award. The award must carry exceptional prestige.
  • A laureate is not self-declared. Someone else — an institution of high standing — must bestow the title.

A laureate is a person who has received an official, prestigious honor from a recognized institution in acknowledgment of their exceptional, distinguished achievement — most famously in the form of a Nobel Prize or a government-appointed poet's title.
9796:
Lava is molten rock — rock so incredibly hot that it has melted into a thick, flowing liquid — that has erupted from a volcano and reached the Earth's surface.

That's the heart of it. But there's a lot more to understand to truly know this word.
The difference between lava and magma

Deep inside the Earth, there are pockets of melted rock. When this melted rock is still underground — sitting in those pockets or travelling through cracks beneath the surface — it is called magma.

The moment that same melted rock breaks through the surface of the Earth (through a volcano, a crack in the ocean floor, or a fissure in the ground), it gets a new name: lava.

So lava and magma are the same substance — it's just about location. Underground = magma. Above ground = lava.
What lava looks like and feels like

Lava in its molten (liquid) state is extraordinarily hot — typically between 700°C and 1,200°C (roughly 1,300°F to 2,200°F). To put that in perspective, the hottest oven in a kitchen reaches about 250°C. Lava is roughly five times hotter than that.

At those temperatures, lava glows. It can range in colour from bright orange-yellow (when freshest and hottest) to dark red (as it begins to cool slightly). As it cools further, a dark grey or black crust forms on the surface, even while the inside remains molten and moving.

Lava is not like water — it doesn't flow that freely. It is thick and heavy, somewhat like slowly pouring cement or even thick honey. However, how fast it moves depends on:

  • How thick (viscous) it is — some lava is runnier, some is almost paste-like
  • How steep the ground is — lava moves faster going downhill
  • How hot it is — hotter lava flows faster because it stays more fluid

Some lava flows move at just a few metres per hour, slow enough to walk away from. Others, particularly thin, runny lava on steep slopes, can race at speeds of 50 km/h (30 mph) or more — fast enough to be genuinely dangerous.

This is important: the word lava actually refers to the substance in two different states:

  1. Molten lava — the liquid, flowing, glowing hot rock while it is still moving or erupting. This is what most people picture when they hear the word.
  2. Solidified lava — the same substance after it has cooled and hardened into solid rock. Once lava stops flowing and cools down completely, it becomes a type of volcanic rock. This rock is also called lava (or "lava rock").

So when someone says "the island is made of lava," they mean it is made of rock that was once molten and has since solidified. When someone says "lava is pouring down the volcano," they mean the liquid, flowing form.
The different kinds of lava flows

Not all lava looks or behaves the same. Scientists and volcanologists (people who study volcanoes) have identified different types based on how the lava behaves and what it looks like after it cools. Two of the most commonly referenced types come from Hawaiian words:

  • Pāhoehoe (pronounced pah-HOY-hoy): This is smooth, shiny lava that forms rope-like or wrinkled patterns as it cools. It flows relatively easily and creates a smooth surface.
  • ʻAʻā (pronounced ah-AH): This is rough, jagged, and clinkery lava with a sharp, broken surface. It is thicker and moves more sluggishly than pāhoehoe. Walking on solidified ʻaʻā is extremely difficult and can cut through shoes.

There is also pillow lava, which forms when lava erupts underwater — the cold seawater causes the lava to cool rapidly into rounded, pillow-like shapes.
What lava becomes — and what it creates

When lava cools and solidifies, it becomes volcanic rock. Different types of lava, cooled in different ways, produce different kinds of rock:

  • Basalt — the most common volcanic rock on Earth, dark grey to black, forms from fast-cooling lava
  • Obsidian — a naturally occurring volcanic glass, jet black and extremely sharp, forms when lava cools very rapidly
  • Pumice — a light, porous rock filled with tiny holes, formed when gas-rich lava cools quickly, trapping bubbles inside. It is so light it can float on water.
  • Scoria — similar to pumice but denser, also full of holes, commonly reddish-brown or black

Over time, solidified lava builds up and forms new land. Many islands — including the Hawaiian Islands and Iceland — were entirely built by repeated lava flows over millions of years. Lava is, in a very real sense, the Earth's way of creating new ground.

Lava can also flow underground through hollow tunnels called lava tubes, which form when the outer surface of a lava flow cools and hardens while molten lava continues moving through the inside. Once the eruption stops and the lava drains out, an empty tube (sometimes kilometres long) is left behind — essentially a natural cave.

The word lava is used as a noun and functions as an uncountable noun in most situations — meaning you usually don't say "a lava" or "lavas." You say:

  • "Lava poured down the mountainside."
  • "The village was destroyed by lava."
  • "The island is made of volcanic lava."
  • "Geologists studied the solidified lava."

It can also be used as a modifier (an adjective-like descriptor) before other nouns:

  • Lava flow — the moving stream of molten lava
  • Lava field — a large area covered by solidified lava
  • Lava tube — the underground tunnel described above
  • Lava lamp — a decorative lamp inspired by the appearance of slowly moving blobs of lava (no actual lava is involved)

Lava is not just a geological curiosity — it is one of the most powerful forces that shapes the surface of our planet. It destroys everything in its path when it erupts (homes, forests, roads), but it also creates fertile soil over thousands of years as volcanic rock breaks down. Some of the most agriculturally rich lands in the world sit atop ancient lava beds.

Lava also exists beyond Earth. Scientists have observed evidence of volcanic activity — and therefore lava — on other bodies in our solar system, including Io (a moon of Jupiter), which is the most volcanically active object known, and on Venus and Mars.

In short: lava is molten rock that has erupted onto the Earth's surface. It is searingly hot, it flows like a thick liquid, it destroys what it touches, it cools into rock, and over vast stretches of time, it builds entire landmasses. The word refers equally to the flowing liquid and the solid rock it becomes once cooled.
9797:
To lave means to wash or bathe something — typically with water, and typically in a gentle, careful, flowing way.

That's the foundation. But there are two distinct uses of this verb, and understanding both will give you the full picture.

When a person (or creature) is the one doing the action, to lave means to wash something carefully, often by pouring water over it, immersing it, or bathing it gently. It implies a deliberate, tender act of cleaning — not a hurried rinse, not vigorous scrubbing, but a thoughtful, gentle washing.

  • She laved the wound with cool water before dressing it. → She carefully washed/bathed the wound.
  • The priest laved his hands before the ritual began. → The priest washed his hands.
  • He sat by the stream and laved his aching feet. → He bathed/soaked his feet.
  • She stepped into the pool and laved herself in its stillness. → She bathed herself.

This is the use you'll encounter most often, especially in poetry and literary prose. When water — a river, the sea, waves, rain — is the subject, to lave means the water flows gently along, laps against, or washes softly over a surface. It's a continuous, unhurried, caressing kind of movement. Not crashing. Not violent. Soft and persistent.

  • The river laves the roots of the ancient willows. → The river flows gently against and washes the roots.
  • Soft waves laved the moonlit shore. → Soft waves gently and repeatedly washed the shore.
  • The rain laved the dusty streets clean. → The rain washed over the streets.
  • Cold water laved the smooth stones at the river's edge. → Cold water flowed against and washed the stones.
The Register: When and Where This Word Lives

You will almost never hear "lave" in everyday speech. Nobody says, "go lave your hands before dinner." They say wash.

Lave is a literary, poetic, and formal word. It lives in poetry, literary fiction, and elevated prose. When a writer deliberately chooses lave over the simpler word wash, they're making a stylistic choice — they want the sentence to feel more graceful, more timeless, slightly elevated in tone.

Notice how the mood shifts:

Waves washed the shore. — Plain, functional, factual.

Waves laved the shore. — Gentle, almost tender, with a soft, unhurried quality.

Same event, different feeling. That gap is exactly why writers reach for lave.

Lave consistently suggests gentleness, softness, and care. Whether a nurse is laving a patient's feverish forehead, or a river is laving a mossy bank, the word implies something slow, soothing, and almost intimate. There is no harshness in lave. It is the word for water that caresses, for hands that tend with care.

This also means it sometimes appears in slightly ritualistic or solemn contexts — a priest washing his hands, a healer cleaning a wound, a person bathing as an act of renewal or devotion — because the gentleness of the word suits those moments.

In very literary writing, you'll occasionally see lave used metaphorically — where something other than literal water does the "washing":

  • Pale moonlight laved the sleeping valley. → Moonlight bathed/washed over the valley softly.
  • A cool breeze laved his skin. → A cool breeze washed gently over his skin.

In these cases, the writer is borrowing the feel of lave — that soft, flowing, enveloping quality — and applying it to light, air, or something similarly gentle and diffuse.

• Nothing to do with lavish, which means generously abundant or extravagant in giving.
  • Nothing to do with lava, the molten rock from volcanoes.
  • In Scottish English and some older Northern English dialects, lave can mean the rest or the remainder ("the lave of the group"), but this is a completely different word that you'd only encounter in Scottish literature or dialect writing. It has no connection to washing.

Lave = to wash or bathe gently, or (of water) to flow softly against something.

  • Person laving something → carefully washing/bathing it with water
  • Water laving something → gently flowing against, lapping over, washing a surface
  • Always implies softness, gentleness, and care — never force or roughness
  • A literary, poetic word — not used in everyday conversation
  • Metaphorically, light or air can "lave" a surface in very literary writing

Whenever you see lave in a poem or a novel, picture water moving gently — either in someone's cupped hands tending to something carefully, or as a river quietly, ceaselessly washing the bank it passes. That image will never mislead you.
9798: As a noun, "lavender" has two main meanings: a plant and a color. Both are connected — the color is named after the plant.

Lavender is a small, bushy plant with long, thin stems that shoot upward and carry clusters of tiny flowers at their tips. The leaves are narrow, small, and silvery-green — almost gray. The plant grows as a low shrub, typically about knee-height, and thrives in warm, sunny, dry conditions.The flowers are almost always a soft purple-blue — gentle, not loud. Some varieties produce white or pink flowers, but the classic lavender is always that familiar soft purple.

What makes lavender truly special, and what it is most famous for, is its scent. Lavender has a strong, sweet, clean, slightly herbal fragrance. Many people find it deeply calming and relaxing. The scent doesn't just come from the flowers — if you rub the leaves or stems between your fingers, they release the same aroma too.

Lavender grows naturally in the Mediterranean region, especially in France, Spain, and Italy. Southern France — a region called Provence — is particularly associated with lavender. Every summer, vast fields there turn entirely purple as the lavender blooms, and this has become one of the most iconic and photographed landscapes in the world.

Because the noun "lavender" can refer to both the live plant and its harvested, dried flowers, it's worth understanding how it is actually used in everyday life:

Fragrance and aromatherapy. This is by far the most common use. Lavender's scent is widely believed to reduce stress, ease anxiety, and help with sleep. You'll find it in candles, room sprays, pillow mists, bath bombs, soaps, and shower gels. The simple act of smelling lavender is a well-known folk remedy for restlessness.

Essential oil. The flowers are processed — usually through steam — to extract lavender essential oil, a highly concentrated liquid that captures the plant's scent. This oil is used in perfumes, lotions, cosmetics, massage oils, and diffusers. It is one of the most widely used essential oils in the world.

Sachets. Dried lavender flowers are placed inside small cloth pouches called sachets. People tuck these into wardrobes, drawers, suitcases, or under pillows to keep things smelling fresh. Lavender also naturally repels moths, which makes it a traditional way to protect stored clothing.

Cooking. Lavender is used as a culinary herb, particularly in French cooking. It appears in a spice blend called herbes de Provence, and on its own in things like lavender honey, lavender shortbread biscuits, and lavender-infused syrups. The flavour is floral, slightly sweet, and a little perfume-like. Because the taste is powerful, only very small amounts are ever used — too much and food tastes like soap.

Herbal teas. Dried lavender flowers are steeped in hot water to make a mild, calming tea. It's often blended with chamomile or other herbs.

Decoration. Bunches of dried lavender are hung in homes as a natural, long-lasting decoration. They hold their color and scent for a long time after drying.

Traditional medicine. Lavender has been used for centuries in folk medicine as a treatment for headaches, insomnia, and minor skin irritations. While modern science supports some of these uses (particularly its calming effect on the nervous system), it is not a replacement for medical treatment.

When "lavender" is used as a noun to mean a color, it refers to a pale, soft, delicate shade of purple — as if you took purple and mixed a generous amount of white into it. The result is a color that feels light, gentle, and airy rather than bold or deep.Think of it this way: if you lined up purple, violet, lilac, and lavender from darkest to lightest, lavender would sit near the lightest end — soft and almost pastel. It is closely related to lilac, though lavender tends to have a slightly cooler, bluer quality, while lilac leans slightly warmer and more pink.

This color is named directly after the flowers of the lavender plant, because that soft purple-blue is precisely what the blossoms look like.

In everyday use, you'll hear people describe things like wedding themes, bedroom walls, clothing, and stationery as "lavender" when they mean this particular gentle purple.

As a noun, "lavender" means one of these three closely related things:

  1. The plant — a fragrant, purple-flowered Mediterranean shrub grown worldwide for its beauty and scent.
  2. The dried flowers or herb — the harvested part of that plant, used in cooking, fragrance, medicine, and decoration.
  3. The color — a pale, soft, delicate shade of purple inspired by the flowers of that plant.

In almost every context you encounter the word, the meaning will be one of these — and often more than one at once, since the scent, the plant, and the color are all so deeply associated with each other that they are nearly inseparable in people's minds.
9799:
Lavish means more than enough — and done with richness, generosity, or luxury. Whenever you see or use the word "lavish," it is pointing at something that goes beyond the ordinary or the necessary, usually in an impressive or extravagant way.

Think of it this way: if something is enough, it is not lavish. If something is a lot, and done in a grand, rich, or generous way, it is lavish.

"Lavish" works on two levels at once, and understanding both is key.

1. Quantity — There is a LOT of it.
Lavish describes something given or existing in very large amounts. Not just a little extra — but abundantly, even excessively.

2. Quality — It feels rich, grand, or impressive.
Lavish is never used for simple, humble things. It carries a feeling of luxury, splendour, or high value. A lavish meal isn't just a big meal — it's a big, spectacular meal.

Both layers usually work together. That's what makes "lavish" special — it captures both the amount and the richness of something.

If you were to walk into a lavish party, you would immediately feel it. The decorations would be stunning and plentiful. The food would be extraordinary in both quality and quantity. Nothing would feel half-done or modest. Everything would feel like no expense was spared. That feeling — of richness, excess, and impressiveness all at once — is what "lavish" captures.
The Full Range of What "Lavish" Can Describe

Things and places:
You can describe physical things and environments as lavish when they are grand, luxurious, and abundant in detail or quality.

A lavish hotel suite — extremely luxurious, with no expense spared.
A lavish wedding — a grand, expensive, over-the-top celebration.
Lavish decorations — rich, plentiful, and impressive.
A lavish feast — a huge spread of extraordinarily good food.

Praise, attention, and care:
"Lavish" is very commonly used to describe how generously someone gives non-material things like compliments or praise.

The teacher gave the student lavish praise — she praised the student enormously and enthusiastically, far more than a simple "well done."
He showered her with lavish attention — he gave her an extraordinary amount of focused care.

Spending and lifestyle:
A person who spends very freely and lives with great luxury can be described as having a lavish lifestyle, or as being lavish with their money.

She led a lavish lifestyle — she lived with great luxury, spending richly on food, travel, clothing, and comfort.

This is a nuanced but important point. "Lavish" is not always negative, but it can carry a subtle suggestion of excess or wastefulness depending on the context.

When used admiringly, it simply means impressively generous or luxurious:
"The hotel gave us a lavish welcome." — This sounds wonderful and positive.

When used with a critical tone, it can imply recklessness or irresponsible excess:
"He spent lavishly on himself while his family struggled." — Here, the excess feels selfish and inappropriate.

So the word itself is neutral — the context and tone around it tell you whether the speaker admires the lavishness or disapproves of it.

Certain words pair with "lavish" so often that knowing them will help you recognise and use it naturally:

Lavish praise / compliments — giving enormous amounts of admiration or positive feedback.
Lavish party / banquet / feast — a grand, expensive, and abundant celebration or meal.
Lavish gifts — extremely generous, expensive, or impressive presents.
Lavish lifestyle — a way of living marked by luxury and free spending.
Lavish spending — spending money very freely and in large amounts.
Lavish décor / setting — richly and impressively designed surroundings.
Lavish attention — giving a very generous and extraordinary amount of focus or care to something or someone.

Knowing near-synonyms helps you feel the exact "weight" of lavish:

Extravagant — very similar to lavish, but leans more toward excess and often carries a stronger suggestion of wastefulness.
Opulent — rich and luxurious, but focuses more on visible wealth and grandeur, slightly less on quantity.
Sumptuous — extremely grand and rich, especially used for food, décor, or physical surroundings.
Luxurious — focused on high-end comfort and indulgence, but slightly softer than lavish.
Generous — similar when lavish describes giving, but "generous" is simpler and has no suggestion of excess.
Abundant / Profuse — captures the large quantity side of lavish, but without the richness or luxury.

Among all these, lavish is the one that most perfectly blends large quantity + impressive richness in a single word. That's its unique strength.

Meagre — very small in amount, barely enough.
Frugal — careful and sparing with money or resources, the opposite of lavish spending.
Modest — not extravagant, restrained, and simple.
Austere — very plain and without luxury or excess.
Sparse — small in quantity, thinly spread.
A Simple Test to Know If "Lavish" Fits

Ask yourself three questions about the thing you want to describe:

  1. Is there a lot of it — more than what's needed or expected? ✓
  2. Does it feel rich, grand, or impressive rather than simple and plain? ✓
  3. Does it carry a sense that no expense or effort was spared? ✓

If you answer yes to all three, "lavish" fits perfectly.

Lavish means: extremely generous, abundant, and rich in a way that feels grand and impressive, often going well beyond what is ordinary or necessary.

It applies to physical things (a lavish banquet), to acts of giving (lavish praise), to spending habits (lavish lifestyle), and to environments (lavish décor). It is usually impressive or admirable, but can carry a subtle note of excess or wastefulness when the context calls for it.
